blocks.text: Fig 15.14 shows the convex surface of a lens in contact with a flat glass plate. A thin film of air forms between the two surfaces. Viewed in monochromatic light, the set-up shows circular interference fringes (Fig 15.15). These were studied by Newton and are called Newton's rings.

blocks.alt: Top left: a ray in air hits a thin film of thickness t and index n; one ray reflects at the top surface and another, after passing into the film, reflects at the bottom; both travel up towards the eye. Top right: an air wedge between two glass plates, separated at one end by a thin spacer of height h, with alternating dark and red fringe marks above. Bottom: Newton's rings: a plano-convex lens resting on a flat glass plate, and concentric dark and light rings with a dark centre.
blocks.caption: Thin films, the air wedge and Newton's rings (original diagram after Figs 15.11 to 15.15).
blocks.long_description: In each case two reflections, from the top and bottom of a thin layer, interfere. The thickness of the layer sets the path difference; where it is nearly zero, the half-cycle shift on one reflection makes the fringe dark.

blocks.text: Newton's rings form when a plano-convex lens is placed on a flat glass plate, so that a thin air film lies between them. Light from a monochromatic source such as a sodium lamp reflects from both the top and bottom surfaces of this air film. The reflected rays interfere constructively (bright rings) or destructively (dark rings), depending on the path difference and the phase shift between them. Newton's rings can be used to find the wavelength of monochromatic light and the radius of curvature of lenses, and in precision optics to detect irregularities in surfaces.
